prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, using bifunctional and glue-type small molecules to recruit E3 ligases and remove chosen proteins.

statement.case_for: I opened with phase separation (B024) because it is the candidate closest to my own physical-chemical way of thinking, but the opening ballots show that targeted protein degradation has by far the broadest and most robust support: four first places and six top-three rankings. On the merits, it is a clean chemical concept (event-driven, catalytic removal of a target by induced proximity) that has produced a new drug modality, and it has independent confirmation across many laboratories and target classes. It also has a quantitative physical-chemical core that I value: ternary-complex formation, cooperativity and catalytic turnover, which is where Ciulli's structural and biophysical work matters. I therefore move B056 to first place in my preferred configuration, with Crews and Deshaies for the concept and early proof of principle and Ciulli for the structural and mechanistic basis that made degraders drug-like.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize would honour a modality whose clinical proof is still arriving, while the credit is more tangled than the three-name limit allows. Handa and Ito (cereblon as the thalidomide target), Sakamoto, Gray and others are all defensible, and any trio leaves out a real thread of the discovery, most obviously the molecular-glue branch. If a degrader is not yet an approved therapy, the committee could be seen as rewarding promise rather than consolidated impact. I also worry that a prize that is again centred on drug-discovery chemistry leaves soft-matter and physical chemistry, where phase separation (B024) and lipid nanoparticles (B052) sit, unrepresented.

responses.point: Daniel ranked B056 first with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target underpins the molecular-glue branch and the CRBN-recruiting degraders.
responses.response: I agree that the cereblon discovery is the real challenge to a Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli trio, and I take it seriously. My qualification is that the PROTAC concept is a designed, generalisable principle, while Handa's work is the discovery of a target mechanism for an existing drug. Both are important, but the second is more naturally credited as a separate achievement. I put Ciulli over Handa because the ternary-complex and VHL-ligand work gives the concept its quantitative, design-level physical chemistry, but I accept that the committee could reasonably choose Handa and I would not block it. We should state the choice and its cost openly in the citation discussion.

responses.point: Heiner ranked B056 first and framed it as a shift from occupancy-based inhibition to event-driven, catalytic removal, with quantitative ternary-complex cooperativity, while noting that the field may be slightly early without an approved degrader.
responses.response: I share this framing and it is what moved me, since cooperativity and catalytic turnover are exactly the thermodynamic and kinetic notions that make this chemistry rather than only pharmacology. I am less comfortable than Heiner suggests with the timing argument cutting both ways: if we wait for an approved drug, we hold a prize hostage to regulatory events that are not what the criterion measures. The concept has been independently reproduced for twenty-five years, which is the maturity that matters to me. I would, however, ask that we state what we mean by the demonstrated impact so that the citation rests on the chemistry.

responses.point: Peter ranked nitrogenase (B060) first for its physical-chemical depth: electron delivery, ATP-gated conformational coupling and a unique FeMo-cofactor with an interstitial carbide, confirmed over decades and still being refined.
responses.response: I find the nitrogenase case scientifically serious and I do not think its lower opening support reflects lower merit, since opening support and merit are different things. Where I differ is on the claim that the story is mature: as Peter says, the catalytic cycle and substrate-binding state are still open, and the attribution across Rees, Einsle, Seefeldt, Dean and Ribbe is also hard to resolve into three names. I would want to understand which single step of the mechanism the citation would credit before I could put it ahead of degraders, but I would be glad to see it discussed as the strongest bioinorganic alternative.

responses.point: Peter Somfai ranked Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling (B051) first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig turned amine arylation into a routine operation used across pharmaceutical and materials synthesis, and noting that the 2010 cross-coupling prize may make some members feel the area is already honoured.
responses.response: I respect the adoption argument, which is as strong as any on the list, and I accept that C-N coupling is a different bond construction from the C-C couplings of 2010. My reservation is the one Peter himself raises: the committee has recently honoured palladium cross-coupling, and a prize here would read as an extension of an existing recognition and not a new concept. I would also note that the credit question around Kosugi is real for a general catalytic method. I would not oppose B051 on merit, and I think it belongs among the alternatives we keep seriously open, but I do not see it as a stronger first choice than a new modality.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will resolve the PROTAC versus molecular-glue credit by including Handa (and possibly Ito) instead of Ciulli
Whether the lack of an approved degrader should delay recognition, and how much weight clinical status should carry in a Chemistry citation
Whether phase separation (B024) is mature enough in physiological terms, since the in vivo relevance of condensates is still debated, and whether the committee treats it as chemistry
How to credit the lipid nanoparticle work (B052) among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and its overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B056, B024 or B052. My research on lipid self-assembly and membranes is close to the lipid nanoparticle topic (B052), and I am a Lund colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, but I have no personal or institutional tie to any credited candidate that I know of.
